Background Myostatin negatively regulates muscle growth, and its inhibition by suitable proteins can increase muscle bulk and exercise performance. However, the reference values of serum myostatin in athletes performing strength training are still lacking. Methods A cross-sectional study recruiting28 male collegiate athletes performing strength training and 29 age-matched normal controls was conducted. The serum concentration of myostatin and insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), grip strength, and body composition were the main outcome measures. We used regression models to analyze the correlation between serum markers and the physiological parameters. The athlete group had greater height, weight, BMI, fat mass percentage, fat-free mass, muscle mass, waist girth, grip strength, and estimated daily energy expenditure. Results The IGF-1 concentration was higher in the athlete group (324 ± 80 vs. 263 ± 134 ng/ml), but the myostatin levels did not differ (12.1 ± 3.7 vs. 12.4 ± 3.5 ng/ml). The reference value for IGF-1 among the healthy young males was 293 ± 114 ng/ml, correlated with age and height; the value for myostatin was 12.3 ± 3.6 ng/ml, correlated negatively with BMI, fat mass percentage, and waist girth after adjustment for age. Conclusion Myostatin level is negatively related to fat percentage, and serum IGF-1 is positively related to height. The reference values could provide a basis for future doping-related study. Keywords Biomarker Doping Exercise Reference value Fat-free mass http://dx.doi.org/10.13039/501100005762 National Taiwan University Hospital NTUH 99-M1401 Han Der-Sheng National Science Council (TW) 97-2314-B-002-014-MY3 Han Der-Sheng issue-copyright-statement © The Author(s) 2017 Background As a member of the transforming growth factor β superfamily, myostatin is a negative regulator of muscular growth and differentiation. Myostatin knock-out mice have three times more muscle mass than their wild-type counterparts [ 1 ]. Better functional performance is also observed without noticeable physiological compromise in these animals. On the other hand, nude mice over-expressing myostatin showed a cachectic phenotype with both skeletal muscle and adipose tissue atrophy [ 2 ]. Myostatin is translated into a 310-amino acid peptide, and cleaved as N terminal propeptide and C terminal active peptide. It is then circulated in the blood as an endocrine hormone [ 2 ]. The N-terminal propeptide is a potent inhibitor for myostatin. In a human study, a male baby born to a professional athlete mother in Germany was found to have a bulky muscle mass and loss-of-function myostatin mutation [ 3 ]. The serum myostatin peptide level was as low as undetectable in this male baby. It is reasonable to hypothesize that inhibiting myostatin can increase muscle mass and strength, and the sports performance of athletes. Another study revealing that the serum myostatin propeptide concentration in a bodybuilder was significantly higher than that in an untrained volunteer supports this hypothesis [ 4 ]. Strength training, a mode of exercise that can increase muscle mass, can modulate myostatin. Strength training inhibits intramuscular myostatin mRNA and protein expression in rats [ 5 ]. In a human study, similar findings were reported by Roth et al. that muscular myostatin mRNA level decreased 37% in healthy volunteers after a 9-week course of heavy unilateral knee extension strength training [ 6 ]. In addition, Walker et al. claimed that the serum myostatin peptide concentration, analyzed with Western blot, decreased 20% in a healthy male volunteer after a 10-week whole body strength training course [ 7 ]. Insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), a downstream molecule of the growth hormone (GH), increases protein synthesis in skeletal muscle. IGF-1 transgenic mice have accelerated skeletal muscle regeneration. The hypertrophic effects of IGF-I infusion on muscle are well documented in animal models and muscle cell culture systems. [ 8 , 9 ] IGF-1 expression increased in a rat model of cardiomyocyte hypertrophy and in healthy volunteers doing strengthening exercises [ 10 ]. Using the C2C12 myotube model, a dose-dependent reduction in myostatin expression was observed on exposure to GH; this action was reversed by the GH antagonist pegvisomant [ 11 ]. We previously proposed that myostatin and IGF-1 could serve as a brake and accelerator mechanism for regulating muscle mass or function [ 12 ]. Based on this accelerator-brake model, we hypothesized that both IGF-1 and myostatin may correlate with lean or fat-free mass. Due to their ability to modulate muscle mass and function, myostatin and IGF-1 genes and their protein products might be a target for doping [ 13 ]. Myostatin-inhibiting antibody and muscle-specific expression of IGF-I were shown to increase the muscle mass and function of mdx mice, an animal model of Duchenne muscular dystrophy [ 14 , 15 ]. It is reasonable to expect improved muscle function after injection of exogenous IGF-1, myostatin propeptide, or myostatin neutralizing antibody, which will change their serum concentrations. However, we still do not have their reference value in the general population or in the athlete. Therefore, we conducted a cross-sectional study to investigate the reference values of serum myostatin and IGF-1 concentrations in male student athletes and untrained counterparts, and secondarily to determine whether relationships with body composition exist for each serum marker in the grouped cohort.

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: Regulation of muscle growth and differentiation, lipid metabolism, cardiac development, regeneration, and physiological adaptations to athletic training and changes in body composition.
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: Myostatin, a myokine and negative regulator of muscle growth and differentiation, affects both muscle and lipid growth. Its inhibition can increase muscle bulk and exercise performance. Myostatin acts through autocrine/paracrine mechanisms and is regulated by extracellular matrix proteins. Strength training can inhibit intramuscular myostatin mRNA and protein expression. IGF-1, a downstream molecule of growth hormone (GH), increases protein synthesis, promotes skeletal muscle regeneration, and has hypertrophic effects, counteracting muscle function decline. Myostatin and IGF-1 are proposed to operate as a 'brake and accelerator' mechanism for regulating muscle mass and function. Exposure to GH can lead to a dose-dependent reduction in myostatin expression. Myostatin has also been observed to influence adipogenesis and may mediate cardiac development.

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary:
A dose-dependent reduction in myostatin expression was observed upon exposure to Growth Hormone (GH) in the C2C12 myotube model, a process reversed by the GH antagonist pegvisomant. Strength training athletes (engaging 
	1 hour/day, five times/week) exhibited higher serum IGF-1 levels compared to untrained controls, while serum myostatin levels did not significantly differ between these groups in a steady state, potentially due to blood sampling timing relative to exercise. Myostatin levels were also elevated in decompensated congestive heart failure patients, decreasing to normal with recompensating therapy. Furthermore, a lifestyle intervention for obese children resulted in myostatin elevation concurrent with reductions in fat mass and BMI. Acute isometric exercise in rats demonstrated a rapid increase in myostatin mRNA within 30 minutes to 6 hours post-exercise, returning to baseline by 24 hours.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: IGF-1 concentration was specifically found to be higher in male collegiate athletes performing strength training compared to age-matched normal controls. Conversely, serum myostatin levels, while not differing significantly between athlete and control groups (including specific sports like weight-lifting and basketball), specifically correlated negatively with BMI, fat mass percentage, and waist girth in healthy young males. However, the specificity and comparability of serum myostatin measurements are challenged by significant variations across studies, primarily due to the use of different ELISA kits. Myostatin itself demonstrates broad effects on both muscle and lipid growth. Furthermore, intracellular myostatin mRNA expression and secretion in isolated muscle tissues may not always faithfully reflect circulating myostatin levels, as evidenced by instances where mRNA changes occurred without corresponding protein changes. Myostatin mRNA expression in cardiac muscle can increase after infarction and exercise but remains unchanged in certain canine models of dilated cardiomyopathy and chronic heart failure, indicating context-dependent specificity. For comprehensive insight, it is recommended to detect serum myostatin in conjunction with other biomarkers such as IGF-1, follistatin, and propeptide rather than relying on myostatin alone.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: Healthy young male Han, including male collegiate athletes (strength training, weight-lifting, basketball) and age-matched untrained college students. Also studied were older men, obese children (6-16 years), non-diabetic Asian Indians, and diabetic patients with metabolic syndrome, central obesity, low high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, and high triglycerides. Populations with specific health conditions included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) patients, chronic heart failure patients (both decompensated and during recompensating therapy), as well as animal models of muscular dystrophy and canine models of dilated cardiomyopathy and chronic heart failure.
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication:
The established serum reference values for myostatin (12.3 
	3.6 ng/ml) and IGF-1 (293 
	114 ng/ml) in healthy young male Han individuals are crucial for future studies on muscle regulation, exercise performance, and the detection of potential doping candidates. These biomarkers show significant correlations with age, height, body composition (BMI, fat mass percentage, waist girth, fat-free mass), and estimated daily energy expenditure, contributing to the understanding of physiological adaptations to sports training. Myostatin levels are implicated in various health conditions: they correlate negatively with fat percentage, BMI, and waist girth in healthy young males. Elevated myostatin is associated with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and decompensated congestive heart failure, while lower levels are linked to metabolic syndrome, central obesity, low HDL-C, and high triglycerides. Lifestyle interventions in obese children leading to decreased fat mass and BMI can result in myostatin elevation. The myostatin polymorphism A55T is associated with higher body fat percentage and adiposity. IGF-1 counteracts muscle function decline and its elevation can indicate sustained activation of the GH-IGF-1 axis, playing a role in muscle growth and regeneration.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: Diagnostic utility (for potential doping detection of myostatin and IGF-1, as an indicator of physiological status in healthy populations, and for monitoring conditions like COPD and heart failure therapy response); Adverse risk (lower myostatin associated with metabolic syndrome/obesity factors; A55T polymorphism associated with higher adiposity; GH/IGF-1 use for performance enhancement relevant to anti-doping); Protective benefit (myostatin elevation associated with decreased fat mass/BMI after lifestyle intervention in obese children, and general relation to muscle growth and performance).

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment:
The study establishes foundational serum reference values for myostatin (12.3 
	3.6 ng/ml) and IGF-1 (293 
	114 ng/ml) in healthy young male Han individuals, which is crucial for future doping-related studies. However, the overall reliability and comparability of serum myostatin measurements are significantly hampered by wide variations in reported levels across studies, primarily due to the use of different ELISA kits (e.g., myostatin ELISA sensitivity is 270 pg/ml with intra-assay <10% and inter-assay <15%). Intracellular mRNA expression and secretion in isolated muscle tissues may not reliably reflect circulating myostatin levels, as evidenced by observed mRNA changes without corresponding protein changes. For IGF-1, ELISA sensitivity is 90 pg/ml with intra-assay 6.7% and inter-assay 6.8%. Further reliability limitations include potential issues with blood sampling timing post-exercise in athletes at steady state, a small sample size impacting statistical power, and potential measurement errors in self-reported physical activity, individual variations in perceived exercise intensity, and BMI-dependent MET values. The current reference values are specific to male athletes in certain sports and require further validation in broader populations.
